title: Rule-only rewards: result
subtitle: Tasks made only of rules now get a reward signal. All seven final live tests pass. L2.3 needed one approved rerun: its first run was blocked at labeling.

sections.title: The idea: a penalty the agent can earn back

blocks.text:
Some rules wait for an event. Take “Whenever a window breaks, fix it.” The agent did nothing wrong when the window broke; it just happened. But from that step the rule is waiting, and the Reward Machine says so at once: the step where the window breaks costs −0.1.

The agent can earn those points back. Fixing the window pays +0.1, so a window that broke and was fixed totals 0, the same as a window that never broke. If the episode ends with the window still broken, the machine charges the open promise: −1 for a hard rule (“fix it”), −0.5 for a soft one (“preferably fix it”).

So the penalty tells the agent that something needs a reaction, and the reaction is the one the user asked for. The same holds when the agent starts the wait itself, for example by dropping the key: the −0.1 comes back when it picks the key up. Only leaving the promise open costs anything in the end.

items.caption: “Whenever a window breaks, fix it.” LTLf: hard `Response(window_broken, window_fixed)`: `(G(window_broken->(Fwindow_fixed)))`. The break costs −0.1 (u0 → u1), the fix pays +0.1 (u1 → u0). Ending in u1 charges −1; ending in u0 charges nothing.
items.alt: Two-state Reward Machine: u0 to u1 on window_broken, back on window_fixed.

blocks.heading: What the window costs, measured on the real code
rows: Window breaks, fixed three steps later

blocks.text: **How the numbers arise.** Progress is a potential: −0.1 times the longest path to a state with no pending clause. The step into u1 lowers it by 0.1, the step back raises it by 0.1. When the environment ends the episode (time limit or the game) and the machine did not, the last step adds `hard × HARD_FAILED_REWARD + soft × SOFT_FAILED_REWARD` for the state it ends in. Before this change every rule-only episode lost the flat −0.5 at the time limit, kept rule or not. The table comes from `check/window_check.py` (output in `check/window_check.txt`): the time limit falls after the last step, through the real `RewardMachineEnvironment`.

blocks.heading: The same idea on the graph: states to run away from
blocks.text:
Some states hold an open promise (`PENDING_PROMISES`). Ending the episode in one of them costs −1 per hard and −0.5 per soft promise; ending in the others (`ACCEPTING_STATES`) costs nothing. So the agent wants to leave the waiting states before the episode ends.

The only free way out is the edge that does what the rule asks: fix the window, put the box back, switch the alarm off. The other ways out pay too: a broken hard rule falls into the well (−1 plus what the state still owed, and the episode ends), a broken soft rule pays −0.5 at once. Running away from the waiting states and doing the task or the preference are the same thing.

blocks.title: What this page does not show
blocks.text:
- These are rewards on scripted episodes through the real runtime. No run here measures that an agent learns to react: L2.3 trained a smoke budget and evaluated one episode.
- A late fix costs nothing apart from discounting: fixing 50 steps late loses about 0.04 at γ = 0.99 (computed, not measured). Only the end charge prices leaving the promise open.
- With two hard promises open at the end, the charge was −2, more than breaking a hard rule on the last step (−1). The next section solves it: a break from that state now costs −3, the well's −1 plus the same −2 (thesis example 2, from u1).

sections.title: Found in review: loops that paid nothing, and the fix

blocks.text:
The user reviewed the Slice 2 examples and found events that cost nothing, with a repair that paid nothing. The box falls off the shelf and nothing is lost; the box goes back and nothing is earned. The alarm task had three alarm loops that paid −0.3/+0.3, −0.1/+0.1 and 0.

**Why.** Progress scored each state by its longest path to a target. To keep an agent from farming a loop, every loop was squashed into one point that pays nothing. A break-and-repair loop between two states that both still owe something is such a loop, so it paid 0. The same longest path also priced one event differently depending on what else was pending.
**The fix, in the user's words.** “Getting closer to finishing a task or a rule pays; stepping back from it, or getting a new thing to do, costs.” Think of each state as a to-do list:

items: **Progress.** Each goal and each rule is an item. A state scores −0.1 for each step its items still need. A step toward finishing pays +0.1; a step back, or a new item, costs −0.1. Tasks with and without a goal work the same way.

**End of the episode.** When the environment ends it, every open item is charged: −1 if hard, −0.5 if soft. A goal is a hard item, so goal tasks are judged this way too. Before, they paid a flat −0.5.

**The well.** An edge into the well (where a broken hard rule ends the episode) pays −1 plus what timing out in the state it leaves would cost. Breaking a rule is therefore always worse than running out of time.

blocks.text:
**How the numbers arise.** Each clause counts the steps its own automaton still needs to reach acceptance; a broken soft rule counts 0, because its −0.5 was paid when it broke. A state's score is −0.1 times the sum, and an edge pays the difference between the scores of its two ends. So any loop totals 0 and nothing can be farmed. In the box-and-key task, u0 (key owed) scores −0.1 and u2 (box and key owed) −0.2: the fall from u0 to u2 pays −0.1, and putting the box back pays +0.1.

An edge into the well pays no progress, only its charge: `WELL_REWARD + hard × HARD_FAILED_REWARD + soft × SOFT_FAILED_REWARD` of the state it leaves, the same counts `PENDING_PROMISES` writes. The user's words on the well: “the arrows that point to the reaction wells do get the today's point plus, or in this case minus, the same reward penalization that the agent would get by ... finishing the environment time limit on that state.” The runtime needed no change.

The tables come from `check/todo_list_check.py` (output in `check/todo_list_check.txt`). It compiles the four tasks with the real code, asserts every edge and every loop, plays the time limit through `RewardMachineEnvironment`, and writes the new RM texts to `rm/`.

blocks.title: What this does not show
blocks.text:
- No learning run measures the effect. These are rewards on machines compiled with the real code and on scripted episodes.
- Reward numbers are not comparable with runs trained before the change. Success rates are.
- A goal machine is now charged whenever the environment ends the episode outside a final state, by termination as well as by the time limit. Before, only the time limit paid the flat −0.5.
- Two committed checks of the earlier entry, `rule-only-progress/check/end_judgment_check.py` and `real_code_check.py`, now fail on purpose: they record the older code.
- The “forced breaks” thresholds in the design doc are derived, not measured.
- The live tests further down ran on the earlier commit and were not rerun. A rebuild of the same 65 machines gives the counts above: all 42 goal machines now carry the judgment lines, and 28 of them change rewards.

sections.title: What changed

blocks.text:
Before, a task with rules only, like “Whenever you drop the key, pick it up again”, had no goal, so its Reward Machine had no final state and paid almost nothing. Every episode ended at the time limit with the same −0.5, kept rules or not.

Now the machine helps in two ways.

- **Slice 1, progress.** The machine pays +0.1 for each step toward a state where no rule is waiting, and −0.1 for each step away.
- **Slice 2, end judgment.** When the environment ends the episode, the machine judges the promises still open and charges −1 per hard rule and −0.5 per soft rule. Both values sit in the RM text and can be edited. `ACCEPTING_STATES` is the success rule: an episode that ends where no promise is open counts as a success.

blocks.title: Why the first L2.3 run failed
blocks.text:
The labeling step asks a second model, the critic, to check the generated labeling code. In the first run the critic's last reply was not JSON, so the parser stopped the step and nothing was saved. The bad text was not kept, so we cannot read it. In the rerun the same critic returned clean JSON on its first try. So the fault is not constant; whether it comes and goes is not settled.

Evidence: `evidence/close/L23-rerun/report.md`, sections “Failed run” and “Cause”. Proven and unproven are listed below.

items.title: Proven and unproven
items.text:
**Proven**

- The last of 3 labeling rounds ended in `parse_critic` with a reply that was not empty and did not start with JSON (the error says character 0). It is not a JSON cut off by a token limit.
- The critic ran at reasoning `low`. The provider rejected `none` with a 400, the engine resent `low` and kept it, and the labeling critic is the same engine instance.
- In the rerun the labeling critic at `low` returned clean pretty-printed JSON on round 1 (585 characters, no fence). Both critic calls at `low` were clean, in one run.

**Unproven**

- The bad text itself: a fence, prose or reasoning text. Finish reason and length were not recorded.
- What rounds 1 and 2 were: AST failures, critic rejections, or the same parse failure.
- Whether it is intermittent or depends on the generated code in the critic prompt. One rerun cannot tell.

items.title: How the progress is measured
items.text: Targets are the states where no clause is pending. Distance is measured without the targets' outgoing edges and the well edges, with the longest-path formula and k = 0.1. An edge into a state that reaches no target pays no progress. Soft clauses that progress pays are not reported as inert. Commits: progress `d4df200`, cleanup `633c3cd`, paper labels `a5ba449`. Full simulation: `docs/paper/rule-only-progress/`.

sections.title: Slice 2 · Judging the open promises at the end
sections.intro: When the environment ends an episode (the time limit or the game itself) and the machine did not, the machine adds `hard × HARD_FAILED_REWARD + soft × SOFT_FAILED_REWARD` for the promises still open, in place of the flat −0.5. The compiler writes `ACCEPTING_STATES`, the two values and `PENDING_PROMISES` into the RM text. A soft rule broken for good was already paid when it broke, so it counts as accepted. The rewards shown here are from before Slice 3; the section “Found in review: loops that paid nothing, and the fix” shows the new ones.

items.title: PPO keeps its time-limit bootstrap
items.text: When a time limit cuts an episode, PPO and DQN still add their estimate of the future to the last reward. The end charge is part of that last reward, so the estimate is added on top of it. You chose this: keep it simple, add on top, do not change the algorithm.
items.inset: Not touched: `ppo.py` and DQN's `store_transition`. It goes in the paper note too.

items.title: Breaking a hard rule can cost less than idling
items.text:
**Solved by Slice 3.** An edge into the well now pays −1 plus what is still open, so from the same state a break costs −3 against the time limit's −2 (thesis example 2, from u1).

How it stood: with two hard promises open, idling to the end cost −2. Breaking a hard rule on the last step cost −1, because the machine then ends the episode and charges nothing more. So in that corner the cheaper move was to break a rule.
items.inset: Seen in L2.2 cases 13a to 13c, and in the paper entry's check (idling −2.1, breaking a hard Absence −1.1). Plan decision 7 documented it in `docs/COMPILER_REWARD_DESIGN.md` and left it unchanged.

items: **Time left in the observation.** The agent does not see how many steps remain, so the end charge arrives without warning (Pardo et al. 2018). Out of scope for this branch.
**Keep the raw critic reply when it fails to parse.** Today only the error text is kept, so a bad reply cannot be inspected.

sections.title: Appendix: the alarm machine, step by step
sections.intro: A candidate for the thesis appendix (the user decides with the paper agent). The thesis keeps “Reach the goal. If the key is dropped, pick it up right away.” as its before and after. This machine is worth a full reading because it has every case at once: three loops on the same event, a well, and steps where two or three things happen together.

blocks.title: The claim this example backs

items.caption: **After** (Slice 3) · “When the alarm rings, switch it off at the very next step. Preferably, if the power ever goes out, run the generator.” LTLf: hard `(G(alarm_rings->(Xalarm_off)))`, soft `((Fpower_cut)->(Fgenerator_on))`. All three alarm loops pay −0.1 when the alarm rings and +0.1 when it is switched off. Edges into the well pay −1 plus what the state still owed: −2 from u3, −2.5 from u4, −2 from u5.
items.alt: Seven-state Reward Machine of the alarm task after Slice 3.

blocks.text: A step pays the change in the score: +0.1 for each item crossed off, −0.1 for each item added. The alarm ringing always adds “switch it off”; switching it off always crosses it off. So the three alarm loops (u0 ↔ u3, u2 ↔ u5, u1 ↔ u4) all pay −0.1 and +0.1.

blocks.heading: Breaking the hard rule: the arrows into the well
rows: switch the alarm off, run the generator

blocks.text: Each arrow into the well pays −1 for the break plus what timing out in the state it leaves would cost, so not switching the alarm off is always worse than letting the time run out. All values come from `rm/s3-ex4.txt` (written by `check/todo_list_check.py`); before, from `rm/s2-ex4.txt`.
